vignette:
At thirty-seven, he is a psychologist who spends his workdays inviting other people to speak about fear, grief, and memory, yet when he begins telling his own story, he does so haltingly, as if each sentence has to pass through a locked gate. He is a married South Asian man, thoughtful and precise, someone who once took pride in being calm under pressure. Before the trauma, he describes himself as busy but grounded: early mornings with tea, a quick exchange with his wife before work, a full day of patients, and evenings spent reading or calling family abroad. He says he used to believe that attention and understanding could make almost anything bearable.

The attack happens on an ordinary weekday. He is in a crowded city clinic building where he sees patients part-time, several floors above the street. He remembers reviewing notes before a session, half-listening to muffled traffic below, when a violent blast tears through the morning. At first, his mind refuses to organize what is happening. The windows shudder, alarms begin shrieking, and the floor seems to jump under his feet. Then come the screams from the corridor and the smell-burning metal, dust, something chemical. He steps into the hallway and sees a man on the ground near the elevators, blood on his sleeve, people running in different directions, no one knowing whether there will be another explosion.

He says his body takes over. He hears himself giving instructions in a voice that sounds strangely detached: move away from the windows, take the stairs, keep low, breathe slowly. He guides two patients and a receptionist down several flights, one hand on the railing, the other steadying a woman who cannot stop crying. Outside, the street is chaos-sirens, smoke, shards of glass, people shouting names into their phones. Later he learns it is a terrorist bombing targeting the block. He also learns that a security guard he greeted almost every week does not survive. What stays with him most is not a single image but a sequence of fragments: a child's shoe on the pavement, the metallic taste in his mouth, the way everyone's faces looked stripped of ordinary expression.

In the first days afterward, he tells himself he is functioning well. He gives interviews to worried relatives, checks on colleagues, and reads every update he can find. He speaks in the composed language he uses with patients-acute stress, nervous system activation, shock. His wife notices he has stopped sitting near windows and startles when a truck hits a pothole outside their apartment. At night he lies rigid beside her, eyes open, waiting for sleep as if sleep itself is unsafe. When he does drift off, he wakes with his heart pounding, certain he has heard another blast. He begins checking the locks more than once, then repeatedly, moving through the apartment in silence.

Over the following weeks, his world narrows in ways he finds difficult to admit. On the train, he scans every bag, every heavy coat, every person who seems restless or withdrawn. If someone raises their voice, his shoulders tense and his jaw locks. He starts leaving extra time for work so he can avoid crowded entrances, but even then he often ends up standing across the street, staring at the building, unable to make himself go in. Once, when a construction noise echoes between buildings, he drops the coffee in his hand and feels immediate shame as strangers turn to look. He tells colleagues he is overtired.

His work changes too. In session, when patients describe violence or sudden loss, he feels pulled out of the room and back into the stairwell, back into smoke and alarms. He begins losing the thread of what people are saying. Sometimes he fixates on whether the office door is closed, whether there is a clear path to the exit. He notices himself becoming impatient with ordinary complaints and then despises himself for it. A patient cries, and instead of feeling empathically present, he hears the crying from that morning after the blast. He compensates by overpreparing, writing meticulous notes, speaking more formally than he used to, as though professionalism can conceal how frayed he feels.

At home, his wife tries to understand the version of him that has returned from the attack. He is physically there but often far away, flinching when she touches him unexpectedly, circling around her questions with abstract answers. Family members call from overseas after seeing news reports about other attacks, and he feels both irritated and guilty when they ask if he is safe. Safe is no longer a word that means anything stable. He stops going to weddings, festivals, crowded restaurants. In places that used to feel familiar, he positions himself near exits and counts the people in the room. He drinks more tea late into the night to avoid sleeping, then feels exhausted and unreal the next day, as if life is happening behind glass.

What troubles him most is that he knows exactly what these reactions mean. He can hear the clinical language in his own head even as he is living it. But knowledge does not loosen the grip of the memories. Months later, a siren can still send a flash of heat through his chest. The smell of burnt wires from an overheated office outlet makes him abruptly nauseated. He still sees the hallway, the blood, the ash in the air. He tells the story carefully, almost academically at first, until he reaches the part about guiding people down the stairs. Then his voice changes. He says he keeps thinking that he got out, and others did not, and on some days that fact follows him into every room he enters.
